title: HIV Rapid Test Kit

hero.heading: HIV Home Test Kit – Rapid Results in 15 Minutes
hero.intro: Test for HIV privately at home with one simple finger-prick blood test. This rapid HIV self-test checks for HIV-1 and HIV-2 antibodies and gives you a result in around 15 minutes. No clinic visit, no sample to post, and discreet delivery across the UK.

questions.question: What is HIV?
questions.answer:
HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) is a virus that attacks the immune system, the part of your body that fights infection. It is passed on mainly through sex without a condom or by sharing needles. HIV can cause no noticeable symptoms for years, so testing is the only way to know your HIV status for sure.

An HIV home test kit lets you check privately. You use a small finger-prick of blood, the test looks for antibodies to HIV-1 and HIV-2, and your result shows in around 15 minutes, with nothing to post to a lab.

questions.question: What are the early symptoms of HIV?
questions.answer:
Some people get early HIV symptoms, a short flu-like illness, 2 to 6 weeks after getting HIV. It usually clears up within 2 to 3 weeks. Symptoms can include:

  • High temperature (fever)
  • Sore throat
  • Swollen glands
  • Skin rash
  • Aching muscles
  • Tiredness
  • Mouth ulcers

These symptoms are common with many other illnesses, and some people get none at all. After this stage, you can have HIV with no symptoms for years while it still affects your immune system. You can’t tell if you have HIV by how you feel, which is why testing matters.

questions.question: Is HIV treatable?
questions.answer: Yes. There is no cure for HIV yet, but treatment is highly effective and free on the NHS. With treatment, people with HIV can expect a similar life expectancy to people without it, and most never reach late-stage HIV (AIDS). Once treatment brings HIV in the blood to an undetectable level, it can’t be passed on through sex. The earlier you know, the sooner treatment can start.

questions.question: Who should take an HIV test?
questions.answer:
You don’t need symptoms to test. It may be worth taking an HIV test if:

  • You’ve had sex without a condom
  • You have a new sexual partner, or more than one partner
  • A sexual partner has told you they have HIV or another STI
  • You’ve shared needles or injecting equipment
  • You have possible symptoms, such as a flu-like illness
  • You’d prefer to test privately

Had a possible HIV exposure in the last 72 hours? Don’t wait for a test result. Contact a sexual health clinic or go to A&E as soon as possible and ask about PEP, medication that can help prevent HIV after exposure.

how.heading: How does the HIV home test work?
how.intro: The test looks for antibodies your body can produce in response to HIV-1 or HIV-2 infection, using a small finger-prick blood sample. Your result appears on the test pad in around 15 minutes, with no sample to send to a laboratory.

steps.title: Prick your finger
steps.text: Wash your hands and clean your fingertip with an alcohol pad. Let it dry, then use the lancet to prick your finger and form a drop of blood.

steps.title: Add blood and diluent
steps.text: Use the pipette to collect your blood and add 1 drop to the sample well marked S on the test pad. Then add 4 drops of diluent (test liquid) to the same well, straight after the blood.

steps.title: Read your result
steps.text: Leave the test pad flat and read your result between 15 and 20 minutes. Don't read the test after 20 minutes, as the result may no longer be reliable.

windows.heading: When should I take an HIV test?
windows.subheading: You can test at any time, but when you get tested for HIV matters. Testing too early can give a negative result even if you have HIV. This antibody test has a 90-day window period, so an early negative should be repeated 90 days after your last possible exposure.
windows.notes:
If you have symptoms or a partner has tested positive, contact a sexual health clinic now.

Possible exposure in the last 72 hours? Contact a sexual health clinic or A&E now and ask about PEP. Don’t wait for a test result.

results.heading: How to read your HIV test result

groups.intro: Read your test between 15 and 20 minutes. Don’t read it after 20 minutes. C is the control line. T is the test line.

notes.title: Good to know
notes.text: This test is designed for screening and doesn’t replace advice from a healthcare professional.

questions.question: How soon after sex can I test for HIV?
questions.answer: You can test straight away, but testing too soon may not detect a new HIV infection. This antibody-only rapid test has a 90-day window period. If you test negative before then, test again at least 90 days after your last possible exposure. A sexual health clinic can offer tests that detect HIV earlier.

questions.question: It’s been less than 72 hours since I may have been exposed to HIV. What should I do?
questions.answer: Contact a sexual health clinic or go to A&E as soon as possible and ask about PEP (post-exposure prophylaxis), medication that can help prevent HIV after exposure. It must be started within 72 hours and works best when started as soon as possible. Don’t wait for a home test result. The clinic will advise you when to test and arrange any follow-up testing.

questions.question: What are the first signs of HIV?
questions.answer: The first signs of HIV, if any, are usually a short flu-like illness 2 to 6 weeks after infection. This can include a fever, sore throat, swollen glands, rash and aching muscles, and it usually passes within 2 to 3 weeks. Many people have no symptoms, so a test is the only way to know.

questions.question: How reliable is the HIV home test?
questions.answer: When used correctly, this test provides a reliable way to check for HIV-1 and HIV-2 antibodies at home. Testing too soon after exposure can affect your result, so a negative result before 90 days should be repeated at least 90 days after your last possible exposure. A positive result isn’t a confirmed HIV diagnosis and needs further testing at a sexual health clinic.

questions.question: How do I use the HIV home test kit?
questions.answer: Clean your fingertip with an alcohol pad and let it dry, then prick it with the lancet. Add 1 drop of blood to the well marked S, immediately followed by 4 drops of diluent (test liquid). Leave the test pad flat and read your result between 15 and 20 minutes. Don’t read it after 20 minutes.

questions.question: How do I read my HIV test result?
questions.answer: One line at C only means negative. Lines at C and T mean positive, even if the T line is faint, and need confirmation at a sexual health clinic. No line at C means the test is invalid and hasn’t worked. Contact us and we’ll help.

questions.question: What does a negative HIV test result mean?
questions.answer: A negative result means no HIV antibodies were detected. If you tested within 90 days of your last possible exposure, test again at least 90 days after that exposure. If you have symptoms or concerns, contact a sexual health clinic for advice about further testing.

questions.question: What if my HIV test result is positive?
questions.answer: A positive result doesn’t necessarily mean you have HIV, so you’ll need another test to confirm it. Contact a sexual health clinic as soon as possible and tell them you’ve had a positive rapid HIV test. NHS sexual health services are free and confidential. If HIV is confirmed, effective treatment is available and people living with HIV can live long, healthy lives. The clinic can also advise you about telling sexual partners.

questions.question: Can I take an HIV test while pregnant?
questions.answer: If you’re pregnant and worried about HIV, speak to your midwife, GP or a sexual health clinic. HIV testing is routinely offered during pregnancy through the NHS. Early diagnosis and treatment can help protect both you and your baby.

questions.question: Can I use this test if I take PrEP or PEP?
questions.answer: If you take or have recently taken PrEP or PEP, speak to your sexual health clinic about testing. These medicines can affect HIV test results, so follow your clinic’s testing schedule rather than relying on this home test alone.

questions.question: What’s the difference between HIV and AIDS?
questions.answer: HIV is the virus. AIDS is the late stage of HIV, which can develop if HIV goes untreated for many years and badly damages the immune system. With treatment, most people with HIV in the UK never develop AIDS.

questions.question: Will anyone know what I ordered?
questions.answer: No. Your order arrives in plain, discreet packaging with nothing on the outside to reveal what’s inside. Your bank statement won’t show “Test Discreet” or the name of the test. We ship within 1 working day.

questions.question: Can I get a free HIV test on the NHS?
questions.answer: Yes. HIV tests are free at NHS sexual health clinics, and some areas offer free postal kits. Clinic samples usually go to a lab and take a few days. Many people choose a rapid HIV home test for a result in 15 minutes, with no appointment and no sample to post.

questions.question: Does this test check for other STIs?
questions.answer: No, this kit only tests for HIV. If you may have been exposed to HIV, you may have been exposed to other STIs too, such as chlamydia, gonorrhoea or syphilis. Many STIs have no symptoms, so it helps to know how STI testing works. Our Core 4 bundle and 7-in-1 STI test bundle check for several in one order.
